claims.text: Bowl is built on wheat straight noodles boiled in a shared pot, with a tonkotsu-shoyu broth and (standard wheat) soy-based tare; no gluten-free preparation exists.

Every bowl uses pork-bone broth and is topped with pork-belly chashu; there is no animal-free option.

name: 熟成細麺 宝屋 西小路五条店 (Jukusei Hosomen Takaraya Nishikoji-Gojo)

claims.text: Wheat ramen noodles are boiled in a shared pot, making the broth and any bowl unsafe for gluten-free diners.
The broth is a shoyu (soy-sauce) tare base, which in standard ramen contains wheat.
All bowls are built on a pork- and chicken-bone broth finished with pork back fat; no plant-based stock is available.
Ramen noodles are wheat-based (one account notes whole-wheat / 全粒粉 flour), so the bowls are not gluten-free and there is no indication of separate gluten-free preparation.
Shoyu and tantan/miso bowls plus duck teriyaki rice bowls and gyoza rely on standard (wheat-based) soy sauce and seasonings; no wheat-free tare is mentioned.
All broths are duck-based and the menu is centered on duck meat throughout, so there is no plant-based broth to protect from cross-contact.
The broth is a tonkotsu-shoyu (pork-bone soy-sauce) base; soy-sauce tare of this kind is virtually always made with wheat.
Broth is simmered from pork bones and chicken carcasses, so all ramen here is animal-based and unsuitable for vegans/vegetarians.
Noodles are explicitly egg noodles (たまご麺) — relevant for both egg and wheat allergies.

name: 広東御料理 竹香 (Kanton Goryori Takeka)

claims.text: No sources address gluten or wheat cross-contamination. As a Cantonese kitchen serving wheat-wrapper spring rolls and soy-sauce-seasoned dishes alongside fried items, cross-contact with wheat should be assumed pervasive.
Signature dishes such as the roast pork are seasoned with soy sauce, and the soy sauce is not specified as wheat-free; standard Japanese/Chinese soy sauce contains wheat.
Vegetable dishes (e.g., the water-spinach stir-fry) are cooked in a kitchen handling pork, crab and other seafood; no vegan separation is indicated.
The kitchen's gentle, aromatics-free Kyoto-Cantonese style means many dishes are lightly seasoned and free of garlic, onion and ginger, which may help diners avoiding those specific ingredients.

name: 廣東料理 平安 (Kanton Ryori Heian)

claims.text: The signature karashi soba uses wheat noodles and the kitchen is a small Cantonese operation cooking many wheat-containing dishes in shared woks, so cross-contact with wheat is effectively unavoidable.
Cantonese/Kyoto-Chinese seasonings and sauces here are based on standard soy sauce and Chinese condiments, which normally contain wheat; no wheat-free soy sauce is mentioned.
The signature dish and broth contain shrimp, chicken, and chicken-kombu stock; the kitchen centers on meat and seafood, so any dish risks animal-product cross-contact.

name: 廣東餐館 鳳飛 (Kanton Sankan Houhi)

claims.text: Kyoto-Chinese noodle and stir-fry dishes here are seasoned with soy-based sauces, which in Japan are standard wheat-containing shoyu; assume gluten is present throughout.
Signature plates are chicken-, pork- and shrimp-based (からし鶏, pork shumai, 酢豚, and the chicken-and-shrimp からしそば), so animal ingredients run through the menu.
House-made wheat noodles are the centerpiece of the shop, so flour and wheat are handled throughout the kitchen and shared boiling water is used for all bowls.
Signature bowls include a shoyu (soy-sauce) ramen, and Japanese ramen soy tare almost always contains wheat-based soy sauce; no wheat-free tare is indicated.
Broths are chicken-based (tori-paitan) and bowls are topped with pork chashu and egg, so all shared soup, surfaces and utensils carry animal products.
